summary: English oak is a large deciduous tree native to Europe and western Asia. Its acorns hang in clusters from a long stalk, a feature behind the name pedunculate oak and one that helps distinguish it from sessile oak. It can live for centuries, while its ecological value grows with age: a 2019 UK estimate linked it with about 2,300 species, including insects, lichens, birds, mammals and fungi.

summary: Common mugwort is an aromatic perennial in the daisy family, native to temperate Europe, Asia, North Africa and Alaska. In temperate regions it spreads mainly through underground stems called rhizomes because few viable seeds are produced. Soil disturbance can break and disperse those rhizomes, allowing fragments to form new plants and making ploughing an ineffective means of control.

summary: Mexican sunflower is an annual or perennial member of the daisy family native to Mexico and Central America, but introduced across much of the tropics. Its fast-growing foliage, green stems and flowers can be cut for mulch or worked into soil as fertilizer; the biomass decomposes rapidly and releases nutrients quickly. In East African sugarcane fields, its flowers are also used to draw beneficial arthropods into a biological-control system.

Oleander-leaf protea is a large shrub or small tree endemic to South Africa. Its cone-shaped flower heads combine pink, carmine, creamy-green or whitish bracts with a distinctive dark, hairy fringe. In its fynbos habitat, periodic wildfire kills mature plants but seeds survive; the small hairy nuts remain packed in the dried flower head before wind carries the released seeds away. Birds and several beetles visit the nectar-bearing flowers.

Erect prickly pear is a large cactus native to tropical and subtropical coastal parts of the Americas. It quickly colonizes hot, open sandy ground, and its purple-red fruits contain dozens of seeds that may remain viable for more than a decade. Birds and mammals disperse those seeds, helping the plant spread; where introduced, it has become invasive in regions including Africa, Australia and southern Asia.

summary: Tantoon is a shrub or tree endemic to eastern Australia, including Lord Howe Island. It has thin bark on smaller plants, while larger specimens develop thicker, flaky bark. Its white, cream, greenish or occasional pink flowers appear singly on short side shoots, mainly from August to January. The resulting capsules can remain attached for several years, giving the plant a long-lasting fruit display.

Gorse is an evergreen shrub native to Western Europe, with green shoots and leaves modified into spines. Its coconut-scented yellow flowers appear throughout the year, especially in spring, and its pods split in hot weather to eject hard seeds that can remain viable for 30 years. Natural oils make the plant readily flammable, but it can resprout after fire and its surviving seeds help it recolonize burned ground.

Armeria sampaioi is a flowering plant in the leadwort family. A 2016–2019 assessment described it as nearly endemic to the mountains of central and northern mainland Portugal, where it grows above 1,000 metres in stony meadows and cracks in granite. That regional assessment classified it as Vulnerable after identifying only five locations, with declining snowfall and trampling among the pressures expected to degrade its habitat.
reviewFlags: Sources differ between endemic to mainland Portugal and nearly endemic; the summary follows the scoped 2016–2019 Red List assessment.

summary: Greater stitchwort is a perennial herb native to western and central Europe, including the British Isles. It grows in woodland, along edges and in open fields, bearing white flowers whose five petals are split about halfway and can look like ten. The long, narrow leaves grow in opposite pairs, with each successive pair set at right angles to the previous one, while the weak stems break easily.

Tansy is a robust aromatic perennial native to Europe and temperate parts of Asia. Upright stems carry dark-green, deeply divided leaves, and in summer it produces small golden-yellow flower heads packed into dense, flat-topped clusters. The strongly scented flowers have also been used in essences and cosmetics, while the plant has a history of both culinary use and folk medicine.

summary: Flax-leaved horseweed is a pioneer plant of tropical and subtropical regions whose precise origin is uncertain, though the source places it most likely in Central or South America. Its narrow, wavy, blue-green leaves and purple-tipped bracts help distinguish it from similar species. It reproduces only by seed, and the lightweight seeds are readily carried by wind, helping it colonize disturbed ground across several continents.
reviewFlags: The wind-dispersal claim in the source is marked citation needed.

summary: Queen sago is a cycad associated with southern India and Sri Lanka. The source says wild plants are known only from southern India while also describing the species as native to Sri Lanka. Its scientific name was formerly applied to several similar Southeast Asian cycads that are now treated as separate species, so older records and uses published under this name may not belong to the modern species.

summary: Xanthosoma violaceum is a tropical American herb in the arum family. Its arrow-shaped leaves have a bluish tone, while the epithet violaceum refers to their violet colour. The source records both the leaves and underground rhizome as food, but only after cooking.

Stinking iris is a flowering plant native across western Europe and parts of North Africa, found in open woodland, hedgebanks and sea cliffs. Its dull blue or buff-yellow flowers last only a day or so, but green capsules remain through winter before revealing scarlet seeds. The common name comes from the beef-like smell that some people detect when its sword-shaped leaves are crushed or bruised.

Chinese redbud is a member of the legume family endemic to China, including southern and north-central regions and Manchuria. Although it can grow as a tree, it is usually found as a shrub. Its nearly circular leaves taper to a point, and the flowers may be pink or milky white. The source also records a long history of using several parts in traditional Chinese medicine.

Wahlenbergia lobelioides is a flowering plant in the bellflower family. The named subspecies W. lobelioides subsp. lobelioides occurs on Madeira and is described as endemic to the wider Macaronesian region.

Nepeta tuberosa is a flowering plant in the mint family. Its named subspecies N. tuberosa subsp. tuberosa occurs in mainland Portugal, where the source describes that subspecies as native and records no protection under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

Agave xylonacantha is an agave native to four Mexican states: Hidalgo, Tamaulipas, Guanajuato and Querétaro. It forms a broad basal rosette of sword-shaped leaves, each ending in a long spine and edged with large teeth that give the margins a wavy appearance. Its flower stalk can rise well above the rosette and carries greenish flowers; its name means “wood spines.”

Macrozamia moorei is a cycad native to Queensland, Australia, and the tallest-growing species in its genus. It can form a trunk up to seven metres tall, topped by keeled leaves as long as 2.5 metres. Each leaf carries 120–220 narrow leaflets, while the short leaf stalks bear numerous spines.

East Asian sage is an annual native to parts of China and Taiwan, where it grows at elevations of about 200–1,200 metres. Its upright stems bear terminal flower clusters with corollas that vary widely in colour, from red and purple through blue to white. Two named varieties differ slightly in the shapes of their leaves and flowers.

Woolly bottlebrush is a shrub or small tree native to South Africa. Its bark changes from smooth and yellowish to grey and deeply furrowed as the plant matures. Woolly undersides on its oval or heart-shaped leaves distinguish it from Greyia sutherlandii, while dense upright clusters of scarlet flowers appear from July to October in its native range.
Eastern dodder is an annual herb in the morning-glory family. The supplied source describes it as a climber with simple, broad leaves.

Azorean heather is a heath endemic to the Azores. Across the archipelago it occupies a striking range of settings, from coastal cliffs, lava flows and dry slopes to native forest, ravines and volcanic craters, and it occurs from sea level to the islands’ highest elevations.

Vanda tricolor is an orchid recorded from Laos and the Indonesian islands of Java, Bali, Lombok and Sumbawa. The plant entered English cultivation in 1846, when collector Thomas Lobb sent it from western Java for Veitch Nurseries.
Frankenia capitata is a flowering plant recorded as native to southern Macaronesia, specifically the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Salvage Islands.
